metadata.description: Enhanced JavaScript Interview Questions - Theoretical depth with How & Why mechanism for 3.5+ years experience
metadata.usage: Merge with javascriptQuestionData.js or import directly for interview prep

enhancedQuestions.question: What is the Event Loop in JavaScript? Explain how and why it exists
enhancedQuestions.answer: The Event Loop is the mechanism that allows JavaScript to handle asynchronous operations despite being single-threaded. Understanding it demonstrates deep knowledge of JS runtime. 📚 HOW it works: 1. Call Stack: JavaScript has one call stack. Synchronous code executes immediately and blocks until complete. 2. Web APIs: Async operations (setTimeout, fetch, DOM events) are offloaded to browser/Node APIs—they don't block the stack. 3. Task Queues: When async operations complete, callbacks go into queues: - Macrotask Queue (Task Queue): setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI rendering - Microtask Queue: Promises (.then, .catch), queueMicrotask, MutationObserver 4. Loop Mechanism: After each macrotask, the engine drains ALL microtasks before the next macrotask. The loop: Execute one macrotask → drain all microtasks → render (if needed) → repeat. 📚 WHY it exists: - JavaScript runs in a single thread—it can only do one thing at a time. Without the event loop, any async operation would freeze the entire app. - The event loop enables non-blocking I/O: while waiting for a network response, the UI stays responsive. - It prioritizes microtasks over macrotasks so Promise resolution happens before the next setTimeout, keeping async flows predictable. 📝 Interview Key: Say "Single-threaded + Event Loop + Task Queues = Non-blocking async." Microtasks run between macrotasks. Know the order: sync code → microtasks → macrotask → microtasks → repeat.
enhancedQuestions.how: Call stack executes sync code; async callbacks go to task queues; loop processes macrotasks and microtasks in specific order
enhancedQuestions.why: Enables non-blocking async in single-threaded JS—UI stays responsive while I/O completes

enhancedQuestions.question: Explain Closures - How do they work and why are they essential?
enhancedQuestions.answer: A closure is a function that retains access to its lexical scope even when executed outside that scope. It's fundamental to understanding JS. 📚 HOW it works: 1. Lexical Scoping: When a function is defined, it captures a reference to its surrounding scope (the environment where it was created). This is stored in the function's [[Environment]] internal property. 2. Scope Chain: When the function executes, it looks up variables in: own scope → outer function scope → ... → global. The outer scope remains in memory as long as the inner function can reference it. 3. Garbage Collection: Normally, when a function returns, its local variables are eligible for GC. With closures, the inner function holds a reference to the outer scope, so it stays alive. 📚 WHY it matters: - Data Privacy: Create private variables—only the returned function can access them. No native "private" in JS before classes. - Partial Application & Currying: Closure captures arguments for later use. - Event Handlers & Callbacks: Handlers often need access to variables from when they were created. Closures preserve that context. - Memoization: Cache object lives in closure scope. 📝 Interview Key: "Closure = function + its lexical environment." The "how" is scope capture at definition time. The "why" is encapsulation, callbacks, and stateful functions.
enhancedQuestions.how: Inner function captures outer scope at definition; outer scope stays in memory as long as inner function references it
enhancedQuestions.why: Enables data privacy, callbacks with context, currying, memoization—core to JS patterns

enhancedQuestions.question: Explain the 'this' keyword - How is it determined and why does it vary?
enhancedQuestions.answer: The 'this' keyword refers to the execution context—who is calling the function. Its value is determined at call time, not definition time. 📚 HOW it is determined: 1. Default Binding: Standalone function call—this = global (non-strict) or undefined (strict). Why? No explicit owner. 2. Implicit Binding: Method call—this = object before the dot. obj.fn() → this = obj. Why? The object is the "receiver." 3. Explicit Binding: call, apply, bind—you explicitly pass this. fn.call(obj) → this = obj. Why? Override default behavior. 4. New Binding: Constructor call—this = newly created object. Why? new allocates and binds. 5. Arrow Functions: No own this—inherits from enclosing lexical scope. Why? Designed for callbacks where you want outer this. 6. Priority: new > explicit > implicit > default. 📚 WHY it varies: - JavaScript's design: functions are first-class; the same function can be called in different contexts. this provides a way to reference the "current" object. - Lost this: When you pass a method as callback (e.g., setTimeout(obj.method)), the receiver is lost—method runs as standalone. Solution: bind or arrow function. - Arrow functions exist specifically to preserve this from the surrounding scope, avoiding the common "this is undefined" bug in event handlers. 📝 Interview Key: "this is decided by how the function is called, not where it's defined." Know the four rules and that arrow functions inherit this lexically.
enhancedQuestions.how: Determined at call time by: default (global/undefined), implicit (object before dot), explicit (call/apply/bind), new (constructed object), or lexical (arrow)
enhancedQuestions.why: Functions are reusable—this lets the same function work with different objects; arrow functions fix lost-this in callbacks

enhancedQuestions.question: Explain Prototype and Prototype Chain - How does inheritance work in JS?
enhancedQuestions.answer: JavaScript uses prototypal inheritance—objects inherit from other objects via the [[Prototype]] link. There is no "class" in the traditional sense; it's a delegation chain. 📚 HOW it works: 1. [[Prototype]]: Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] (accessed via __proto__ or Object.getPrototypeOf). When you access obj.property, the engine looks at obj, then its prototype, then that prototype's prototype, until null. 2. Constructor's prototype: Functions have a .prototype property. When you call new Foo(), the new object's [[Prototype]] is set to Foo.prototype. So Foo.prototype is the template for instances. 3. Chain: obj → Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) → ... → Object.prototype → null. If a property isn't found, you get undefined. 4. Own vs Inherited: obj.hasOwnProperty('x') is true only if 'x' is on obj itself, not on the chain. 📚 WHY this design: - JavaScript was designed to be simple and flexible. Prototypes allow dynamic inheritance—you can add methods to Foo.prototype and all instances get them without re-instantiation. - No classes initially—Brendan Eich modeled it after Self (prototype-based). ES6 classes are syntactic sugar over prototypes. - Sharing: Methods on the prototype are shared; only instance-specific data lives on the object. Memory efficient. 📝 Interview Key: "Inheritance = prototype chain lookup. new sets [[Prototype]] to Constructor.prototype. Classes compile down to constructor + prototype."
enhancedQuestions.how: Property lookup walks [[Prototype]] chain; new sets instance.[[Prototype]] = Constructor.prototype; methods shared via prototype
enhancedQuestions.why: Dynamic, flexible inheritance; memory efficiency (shared methods); JS's original OO model before classes

enhancedQuestions.question: Explain call, apply, and bind - How do they work and why use each?
enhancedQuestions.answer: These are methods on Function.prototype that let you control the 'this' value and how arguments are passed. They're essential for function invocation control. 📚 HOW they work: 1. call(thisArg, arg1, arg2, ...): Invokes the function immediately with this = thisArg and arguments passed individually. fn.call(obj, 1, 2). 2. apply(thisArg, [args]): Same as call but arguments as a single array. fn.apply(obj, [1, 2]). Useful when you have an array of args. 3. bind(thisArg, arg1, arg2, ...): Returns a new function with this and optional args pre-filled. Does NOT invoke. const bound = fn.bind(obj); bound(); 📚 WHY use each: - call: When you want to invoke immediately with explicit this. Common for borrowing methods: Array.prototype.slice.call(arrayLike). - apply: When args are in an array—e.g., Math.max.apply(null, arr) before spread: Math.max(...arr). Or forwarding arguments. - bind: When you need a function to call later with a fixed this (e.g., event handlers, setTimeout). Prevents "lost this." Also used for partial application (currying). 📝 Interview Key: "call/apply invoke now; bind returns a new function. call takes args individually; apply takes an array."
enhancedQuestions.how: All set this explicitly; call/apply invoke immediately (call=individual args, apply=array); bind returns new function with this and optional args fixed
enhancedQuestions.why: Control this in callbacks; borrow methods from other objects; partial application

enhancedQuestions.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)? How and why does it exist?
enhancedQuestions.answer: The Temporal Dead Zone is the period between entering scope and the declaration line where let/const variables cannot be accessed—access throws ReferenceError. 📚 HOW it works: 1. Hoisting: let and const are hoisted—the engine knows they exist from the start of their block. But they are not initialized. 2. TDZ: From the start of the block until the line where let x = ... runs, x is in the TDZ. console.log(x) in that window throws "Cannot access 'x' before initialization." 3. Contrast with var: var is hoisted AND initialized with undefined. So you can access it (as undefined) before the line. let/const stay "uninitialized" until the declaration runs. 4. typeof: typeof x in TDZ also throws (unlike undeclared vars where typeof returns 'undefined'). 📚 WHY it exists: - Prevent use-before-declaration bugs: With var, you could accidentally use a variable before it's assigned, getting undefined. TDZ forces you to declare before use. - Const correctness: const must be initialized at declaration. TDZ ensures you never read it before that initialization. - Block scoping clarity: Makes the "declaration point" explicit—no silent undefined from hoisting. 📝 Interview Key: "TDZ = time between scope start and declaration where let/const exist but are uninitialized. Access throws ReferenceError. Exists to prevent use-before-init bugs."
enhancedQuestions.how: let/const are hoisted but not initialized; from block start to declaration line they're in TDZ; access throws ReferenceError
enhancedQuestions.why: Prevent use-before-declaration; enforce const initialization; make block scope behavior predictable

enhancedQuestions.question: Explain Promises - How do they work under the hood and why do we need them?
enhancedQuestions.answer: A Promise is an object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. It has three states: pending, fulfilled, rejected. 📚 HOW they work: 1. Creation: new Promise((resolve, reject) => {...}). The executor runs immediately. You call resolve(value) or reject(reason) when done. 2. State: Once settled (fulfilled or rejected), the state is immutable. Pending → fulfilled or rejected. 3. Microtask Queue: .then/.catch callbacks are queued as microtasks. They run after the current synchronous code and before the next macrotask. This is why Promise.then runs before setTimeout(0). 4. Chaining: .then returns a new Promise. If the callback returns a value, the new Promise resolves with it. If it returns a Promise, that Promise's outcome is adopted. 5. Error Propagation: Rejected Promises propagate down the chain until caught. Unhandled rejections can trigger unhandledrejection. 📚 WHY we need them: - Callback hell: Nested callbacks become unreadable. Promises allow sequential .then chains. - Composition: Promise.all, Promise.race, Promise.allSettled—compose async operations cleanly. - Error handling: Single .catch at the end vs try-catch in every callback. - Guaranteed async: .then always runs asynchronously (microtask), so consistent ordering with other async code. 📝 Interview Key: "Promise = eventual value + microtask scheduling. .then queues microtask; chaining returns new Promise. Solves callback hell and enables composition."
enhancedQuestions.how: Executor runs sync; resolve/reject change state; then/catch enqueue microtasks; chaining creates new Promises
enhancedQuestions.why: Avoid callback hell; compose async ops (all/race); centralized error handling; predictable async order
enhancedQuestions.codeExample:
const p = new Promise((res) => setTimeout(() => res(1), 100));
p.then(v => v + 1).then(console.log); // 2

enhancedQuestions.question: Explain Pass by Value vs Pass by Reference - What actually happens in JS?
enhancedQuestions.answer: Technically, JavaScript is always pass-by-value—but for objects, the "value" passed is a reference (memory address). So we say "primitives by value, objects by reference" for practicality. 📚 HOW it works: 1. Primitives (number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint): The actual value is copied. Changes inside the function don't affect the original. Modifying the parameter creates a new local value. 2. Objects (including arrays, functions): The reference (pointer) is copied. Both the caller and the function point to the same object. Mutating properties (obj.x = 5) affects the original. Reassigning the parameter (param = {}) does NOT affect the original—you're only changing what the local variable points to. 3. Immutability: To "not mutate" an object, you create a copy (spread, Object.assign, structuredClone) and pass or return that. 📚 WHY this design: - Primitives are small; copying is cheap. Objects can be large; copying would be expensive. Passing a reference is efficient. - The "reference is a value" nuance: You can't make the outer variable point to a new object from inside the function. The reference itself is passed by value. This prevents some bugs (callee can't replace your object) but allows mutation. 📝 Interview Key: "Everything is pass-by-value. For objects, the value is the reference. Reassigning the parameter doesn't affect the original; mutating the object does."
enhancedQuestions.how: Primitives: value copied; Objects: reference (pointer) copied; mutation affects original, reassignment of param does not
enhancedQuestions.why: Efficiency (no large copies); prevents callee from replacing caller's object; allows mutation when needed

enhancedQuestions.question: Explain Event Bubbling and Event Capturing - How does the DOM event flow work?
enhancedQuestions.answer: DOM events flow through three phases: capturing → target → bubbling. Understanding this is key for event delegation and stopPropagation. 📚 HOW it works: 1. Capturing Phase: Event travels from window down to the target element. Rarely used; addEventListener third argument (true) enables it. 2. Target Phase: Event reaches the target element. Handlers on the target run (whether capturing or bubbling). 3. Bubbling Phase: Event travels back up from target to window. Default behavior for most events (click, etc.). Handlers run in reverse order of capturing. 4. stopPropagation(): Stops the event from propagating to parent/child. Doesn't prevent default (e.g., link navigation)—use preventDefault() for that. 5. stopImmediatePropagation(): Stops other listeners on the same element from firing too. 📚 WHY it exists: - Event Delegation: Attach one listener on a parent, handle events from many children. Uses bubbling—child events bubble to parent. Check event.target to see which child. - Historical: Netscape used capturing; IE used bubbling. W3C combined both. Bubbling is more intuitive for most use cases. - Control: stopPropagation when you don't want a parent handler to run (e.g., modal overlay click). 📝 Interview Key: "Three phases: capture (top-down), target, bubble (bottom-up). Default is bubbling. Event delegation uses bubbling + event.target."
enhancedQuestions.how: Event flows: capture (window→target) → target → bubble (target→window); addEventListener 3rd arg true = capture
enhancedQuestions.why: Event delegation (one listener for many children); historical Netscape/IE compatibility; fine-grained control

enhancedQuestions.question: What is the difference between == and ===? Why does == behave unpredictably?
enhancedQuestions.answer: === is strict equality—no type conversion. == is loose equality—JavaScript coerces types before comparing, which leads to surprising results. 📚 HOW == coercion works: 1. If types are same, use SameValueComparison (like ===). 2. If one is null and one undefined → true. 3. Number vs String: string is converted to number. '5' == 5 → ToNumber('5') = 5 → true. 4. Boolean vs any: boolean converted to number (true→1, false→0). true == 1 → true. 5. Object vs primitive: object converted to primitive (valueOf/toString). [2] == 2 can be true (array toString gives '2'). 6. Symbols never coerce—Symbol() == Symbol() is always false. 📚 WHY == is problematic: - Unexpected pairs: 0 == false, '' == false, null == undefined. Makes intent unclear. - Debugging: Bugs from accidental coercion (e.g., comparing user input '' to 0). - Best practice: Use === everywhere. Use == only when you explicitly want null/undefined equality (value == null). - Explicit is better: If you need coercion, do it explicitly: Number(x) === 5. 📝 Interview Key: "=== no coercion; == coerces (string→number, boolean→number, object→primitive). Prefer ===. Know: null == undefined is true."
enhancedQuestions.how: == applies Abstract Equality: null==undefined; string/number/boolean coerced via ToNumber; object via ToPrimitive
enhancedQuestions.why: Legacy flexibility; causes bugs—prefer ===; use == only for null/undefined check (value == null)
enhancedQuestions.codeExample:
'' == 0    // true
'0' == 0   // true
false == 0 // true
null == undefined // true

newQuestions.question: What is the difference between Microtasks and Macrotasks in the Event Loop?
newQuestions.answer: Macrotasks (Task Queue): setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate (Node), I/O, UI rendering. Microtasks: Promise.then/catch/finally, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver. How: After each macrotask, the engine runs ALL microtasks before the next macrotask. Microtasks can enqueue more microtasks—they're all drained before continuing. Why it matters: Promise callbacks run before setTimeout(0). This affects order of execution in async code. Nested microtasks can starve macrotasks if not careful.
newQuestions.how: One macrotask runs; then all microtasks; then next macrotask; microtasks have higher priority
newQuestions.why: Promises resolve before next timer; keeps async flow predictable; MutationObserver before paint

newQuestions.question: What are WeakMap and WeakSet? How do they differ from Map and Set?
newQuestions.answer: WeakMap and WeakSet hold weak references to keys—if nothing else references the key, it can be garbage collected. How: WeakMap keys must be objects; WeakSet values must be objects. No iteration (no keys(), values(), forEach). No size property. When the object-key is no longer referenced, the entry is removed automatically. Why: Avoid memory leaks when storing metadata about DOM nodes or objects you don't own. Map/Set would prevent GC of keys; WeakMap/WeakSet allow it.
newQuestions.how: Keys/values must be objects; no strong reference from collection to key; GC can collect key when no other refs
newQuestions.why: Store metadata for DOM nodes or 3rd-party objects without preventing GC; avoid memory leaks

newQuestions.question: What is the purpose of Symbol in JavaScript? When would you use it?
newQuestions.answer: Symbol creates a unique, immutable primitive—every Symbol() is different. Used for unique property keys and well-known symbols (Symbol.iterator, Symbol.toStringTag). How: const s = Symbol('desc'); obj[s] = 1. Keys from Symbol never clash with string keys. Symbol.for('key') creates/returns a global symbol; Symbol.keyFor(s) gets the key. Why: Private-like properties (without true private fields); defining iterators (Symbol.iterator); adding metadata that won't conflict with user properties; preventing name collisions in libraries.
newQuestions.how: Symbol() returns unique value; use as object key; Symbol.for creates global registry; well-known symbols define behavior
newQuestions.why: Avoid property name collisions; define iterators; metadata; simulate private properties before #fields

newQuestions.question: Explain the difference between Object.create, new, and object literal
newQuestions.answer: Object literal {}: Creates object with Object.prototype. Quick, common. new Constructor(): Creates object, sets [[Prototype]] = Constructor.prototype, runs constructor, returns it. Object.create(proto): Creates object with [[Prototype]] = proto. No constructor. Use for pure prototypal inheritance or creating object without constructor. How: Object.create(null) creates object with null prototype—no inherited props (e.g., no toString). new Foo() is equivalent to Object.create(Foo.prototype) + Foo.call(obj). Why: Object.create for composition, factory patterns, or when you want explicit prototype without constructor. new for class-like instantiation.
newQuestions.how: Literal: default Object.prototype. new: Constructor.prototype + constructor run. Object.create: set proto directly, no constructor.
newQuestions.why: Object.create for flexible inheritance; new for OOP; literal for simple objects

newQuestions.question: What is the Execution Context and what does it contain?
newQuestions.answer: Execution context is the environment in which code runs. Each function call creates a new context. How: Contains: Variable Environment (var, function declarations), Lexical Environment (let, const, block scope), this binding, outer reference (scope chain). Global and function contexts differ. Eval has its own. Why: Explains scoping, closures, and this. Creation phase: hoisting, this binding. Execution phase: code runs. Understanding this helps debug scope and closure issues.
newQuestions.how: Creation: hoisting, this, outer env. Execution: run code. Each call = new context with its own variable/lexical env.
newQuestions.why: Underpins scope, closures, this; explains hoisting and why let/const behave differently

newQuestions.question: What is the difference between setTimeout(fn, 0) and queueMicrotask?
newQuestions.answer: setTimeout(fn, 0): Schedules fn in the macrotask queue. Runs after current sync code and all microtasks. Minimum delay is often 4ms (browser clamp). queueMicrotask(fn): Schedules fn in the microtask queue. Runs after current sync code, before next macrotask. No minimum delay. How: queueMicrotask runs sooner—before any setTimeout(0). Use when you need "as soon as possible" after current sync code, without blocking. setTimeout for true deferral to next event loop tick. Why: queueMicrotask for Promise-like timing; setTimeout for yielding to browser (e.g., allow render).
newQuestions.how: queueMicrotask → microtask queue, runs before next macrotask; setTimeout → macrotask queue
newQuestions.why: queueMicrotask = ASAP after sync; setTimeout = next tick, allows render

newQuestions.question: What is the difference between Map and Object? When to use each?
newQuestions.answer: Object: Keys are strings (or Symbols). Prototype chain. No guarantee of key order (though modern engines preserve insertion order for string keys). No size property. Map: Keys can be any value (object, function). Guaranteed insertion order. .size, .has, .get, .set, .delete. Iterable. No prototype pollution. How: Map is purpose-built for key-value storage. Object is for general-purpose objects with string keys. Why use Map: Object keys, need insertion order, frequent add/delete, store metadata keyed by object. Why Object: simple data, JSON-serializable, prototype needed.
newQuestions.how: Map: any key type, ordered, iterable, size. Object: string/Symbol keys, prototype, JSON-friendly.
newQuestions.why: Map for generic lookup, object keys, order; Object for domain models, JSON
newQuestions.codeExample:
const m = new Map();
m.set({}, 'val'); // object as key

newQuestions.question: What is the Reflect API and why would you use it?
newQuestions.answer: Reflect is a built-in object providing methods for interceptable JavaScript operations. Methods mirror Proxy traps (get, set, has, deleteProperty, etc.). How: Reflect.get(obj, key), Reflect.set(obj, key, val), Reflect.has(obj, key), Reflect.construct(ctor, args), etc. Many return booleans for success/failure instead of throwing. Why: Used with Proxy—forward default behavior: return Reflect.get(target, key) in a get trap. Cleaner than manual implementation. Reflect.construct for new without syntax. Reflect.apply for function calls. Standardizes meta-operations.
newQuestions.how: Reflect methods match Proxy traps; call them to get default behavior; return success/failure as boolean
newQuestions.why: Proxy handlers need to forward to target; Reflect provides standard default; avoids throwing for failures

newQuestions.question: Explain the difference between async/await and Promise.then
newQuestions.answer: Both handle Promises. async/await is syntactic sugar—makes async code look synchronous. .then is explicit chaining. How: async function wraps return in Promise; await pauses until Promise settles. Under the hood, await uses generators/coroutines. .then chains return Promises. Why async/await: Readability, sequential logic, try/catch for errors. Why .then: parallel with Promise.all, when you need the Promise (e.g., return fetch().then(...)), or in non-async contexts. Often combine: await Promise.all([...]).
newQuestions.how: async returns Promise; await suspends, resumes when Promise settles; compiles to generator-like state machine
newQuestions.why: Readability; try/catch; sequential flow; .then for parallel or when returning raw Promise

newQuestions.question: What is the difference between for...in and for...of?
newQuestions.answer: for...in: Iterates over enumerable property keys of an object (including inherited). Returns keys (strings). Use for objects. for...of: Iterates over iterable values (arrays, strings, Map, Set, arguments). Uses [Symbol.iterator]. Use for collections. How: for (const k in obj) → k is key. for (const v of arr) → v is value. for...in can include prototype props; use hasOwnProperty to filter. for...of requires iterable (object with [Symbol.iterator]). Why: for...in for object keys; for...of for array/collection values. Mixing them causes bugs (for...in on array gives indices as strings; for...of on plain object throws).
newQuestions.how: for...in: object keys, enumerable, includes inherited. for...of: iterable values via Symbol.iterator.
newQuestions.why: for...in for object keys; for...of for array/collection values; different use cases
newQuestions.codeExample:
for (const k in {a:1}) {} // k='a'
for (const v of [1,2,3]) {} // v=1,2,3

newQuestions.question: What is the purpose of Object.defineProperty and property descriptors?
newQuestions.answer: Object.defineProperty lets you define or modify a property with fine-grained control over writable, enumerable, configurable. How: Object.defineProperty(obj, 'prop', { value: 1, writable: false, enumerable: true, configurable: false }). Data descriptors: value, writable. Accessor descriptors: get, set. configurable: false prevents redefinition and deletion. Why: Create read-only props, non-enumerable props (hidden from for...in), getters/setters. Vue 2 used this for reactivity. defineProperties for multiple. Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor to inspect.
newQuestions.how: Pass descriptor {value, writable, enumerable, configurable} or {get, set, enumerable, configurable}
newQuestions.why: Control mutability, visibility, getters/setters; foundation for reactivity in Vue 2

newQuestions.question: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy? How to implement each?
newQuestions.answer: Shallow copy: Top-level copied; nested objects/arrays are shared (same reference). Spread, Object.assign, Array.slice create shallow copies. Deep copy: Recursively copy all levels. Nested objects are new. JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) works for JSON-serializable data (no functions, Date, undefined). structuredClone (modern) handles more types. Libraries (lodash cloneDeep) for edge cases. How: Shallow: {...obj}, [...arr], Object.assign({}, obj). Deep: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) or structuredClone(obj). Why: Shallow when you won't mutate nested. Deep when you need full independence. Shallow is faster; deep is safer for nested mutation.
newQuestions.how: Shallow: spread/assign copies top-level refs. Deep: JSON or structuredClone recursively copies.
newQuestions.why: Shallow for simple data; deep when nested mutation must not affect original

newQuestions.question: What are tagged template literals? How do they work?
newQuestions.answer: Tagged templates are function calls with template literals: tag`Hello ${name}`. The tag function receives an array of strings and the interpolated values. How: function tag(strings, ...values). strings = ['Hello ', '!'] for `Hello ${name}!`. values = [name]. Can return anything (string, object). Why: Used for sanitization (prevent XSS), i18n, styled-components (CSS-in-JS), SQL builders, custom parsing. You control how the template is processed.
newQuestions.how: tag`...` calls tag(strings, ...values); strings = split by interpolations; values = interpolated expressions
newQuestions.why: Custom processing: sanitization, i18n, CSS-in-JS, SQL; full control over output

newQuestions.question: What is the difference between null and undefined? When to use each?
newQuestions.answer: undefined: Variable declared but not assigned; missing property; function with no return; optional param not passed. Type: undefined. null: Intentional absence of value. You assign it. Type: object (historical quirk). How: typeof undefined === 'undefined'; typeof null === 'object'. Both are falsy. Use value == null to check both (== null is true for null and undefined). Why: undefined = "not set"; null = "explicitly empty." APIs use null for "no result" (e.g., document.getElementById). Use undefined for optional; null when you want to clear a value.
newQuestions.how: undefined = uninitialized/missing; null = explicit empty; both falsy; value == null catches both
newQuestions.why: undefined = default; null = intentional empty; API design: null for no result
newQuestions.codeExample:
let a; console.log(a); // undefined
let b = null; // explicitly empty

newQuestions.question: How does the optional chaining (?.) and nullish coalescing (??) operator work?
newQuestions.answer: ?. (optional chaining): Short-circuits if left side is null/undefined. obj?.a?.b returns undefined instead of throwing if obj or obj.a is null/undefined. ?? (nullish coalescing): Returns right side only when left is null or undefined. Unlike ||, 0 and '' are not replaced. a ?? b → a if a is not null/undefined, else b. How: obj?.prop, obj?.[expr], fn?.(). ?? has low precedence; use parens with && or ||. Why: ?. avoids verbose if (obj && obj.a) checks. ?? when you want to keep 0 or '' as valid (e.g., count ?? 0 for default only when null/undefined).
newQuestions.how: ?. returns undefined if left is null/undefined; ?? returns right only when left is null or undefined
newQuestions.why: ?. = safe nested access; ?? = default without replacing 0 or ''

newQuestions.question: What is the difference between Error boundaries and try-catch in JavaScript?
newQuestions.answer: Note: Error boundaries are a React concept. In plain JS: try-catch: Catches synchronous errors and rejected Promises only if you await them. Cannot catch errors in async callbacks (e.g., setTimeout) that run later. React Error Boundaries: Class components with componentDidCatch/getDerivedStateFromError. Catch errors in child component tree during render, lifecycle, constructors. Cannot catch errors in event handlers or async code—use try-catch there. How: Wrap sync code in try-catch. For async, use try-catch with await. In React, wrap tree in . Why: try-catch is for synchronous and awaited async. Error boundaries are for React's render phase. Different layers.
newQuestions.how: try-catch: sync + awaited async. Error boundaries: React render/lifecycle errors in children.
newQuestions.why: try-catch can't catch render errors in React; error boundaries isolate UI failures

newQuestions.question: What is the difference between let/const temporal dead zone and var hoisting?
newQuestions.answer: var hoisting: Declaration moved to top of function scope; initialized with undefined. Can access before line (as undefined). Redeclarable. let/const TDZ: Hoisted to top of block but not initialized. From block start to declaration = TDZ. Access throws ReferenceError. Not redeclarable in same scope. How: var: use before declare = undefined. let/const: use before declare = ReferenceError. const must be initialized at declaration. Why: TDZ prevents use-before-declaration bugs. var's "undefined" behavior was error-prone. let/const make temporal dependency explicit.
newQuestions.how: var: hoisted + init undefined. let/const: hoisted, uninitialized until declaration (TDZ); access in TDZ = ReferenceError
newQuestions.why: TDZ prevents use-before-declaration; const requires init; block scoping clarity
newQuestions.codeExample:
console.log(x); var x=1; // undefined
console.log(y); let y=1; // ReferenceError

newQuestions.question: What is the Module pattern and how does it relate to ES modules?
newQuestions.answer: Module pattern (IIFE): (function() { let private = 1; return { get() { return private; } }; })(). Creates closure for private state; returns public API. ES Modules: import/export. Each file is a module with its own scope. Static structure—imports resolved at parse time. Tree-shakeable. Async loading. How: IIFE: wrap in (function(){ ... })(); return public object. ES: export const x; import { x } from 'file'. Why: IIFE was the pre-ES6 way to encapsulate. ES modules are native, static, better for bundlers. Still use IIFE for scripts that must run in non-module environment.
newQuestions.how: IIFE: closure + return. ES: file scope, export/import, static analysis.
newQuestions.why: IIFE for pre-ES6 encapsulation; ES modules for native, tree-shakeable, static modules

newQuestions.question: Explain the difference between static and instance methods in JavaScript classes
newQuestions.answer: Instance methods: Defined on the prototype. Called on instances. Have access to this (the instance). Static methods: Defined with static keyword. Live on the constructor. Called as Class.method(). No this to instance; use for utility/工厂 methods. How: class Foo { m() {} static s() {} }. Foo.s(); new Foo().m(). Why: Instance methods operate on instance state. Static methods for factory (Object.create), utilities (Array.isArray), or methods that don't need instance data.
newQuestions.how: Instance: on prototype, this = instance. Static: on constructor, no instance this.
newQuestions.why: Instance = per-object behavior; static = class-level utilities, factories
newQuestions.codeExample: class C { static create() { return new C(); } }

newQuestions.question: What is the difference between reduce, reduceRight, and fold?
newQuestions.answer: reduce: Left-to-right. arr.reduce((acc, val, i, arr) => ..., initial). Single value from array. reduceRight: Right-to-left. Same signature, processes from end. Useful when order matters (e.g., composing functions). fold: General term (from FP) for reducing a structure to a value. JS uses "reduce" as the name. reduceRight is a fold from the right. How: reduce: acc = f(acc, arr[0]), then f(acc, arr[1]), ... reduceRight: start from arr[arr.length-1]. Why: reduce for sums, flatten, groupBy. reduceRight when right-associative (e.g., compose(f,g,h) = f(g(h(x)))).
newQuestions.how: reduce: left-to-right accumulation; reduceRight: right-to-left; both take (acc, val) => newAcc
newQuestions.why: reduce for common aggregations; reduceRight when order/associativity matters
